status.text: Non-authoritative. CONTEXT.md and ARCHITECTURE.md are the specification; this file records why, and is a suggestion to a reader rather than a constraint on one. Where it disagrees with the two specs, the specs win.

database.text: Omitted; the dataset is too small to need one, and local JSON files stay directly usable as context for local AI tools.

decision records.text: No ADR directory -- this file is deliberately mutable and consolidated, not a set of immutable per-decision files. Decisions carry a stable id (`D1`-`D48`; a gap means a withdrawn decision, numbers never reused) and a `terms` tag array for topical lookup. Tags rather than a single key, since a decision usually relates to more than one term. Superseded reasoning is deleted in place; git holds what was thought before.

display-role key.text: Schema keys name how a value is displayed rather than what it means in a source domain, so a tile mapper can retarget new source data onto an existing registry item without new code.

D1.text: One interface for changing a dashboard; a person's client and an agent are peers over it, not a privileged path each. Rejected: an agent reaching persistence directly, or duplicating permission logic -- either creates a second door a permission check doesn't cover.

D2.text: `role` is a named bundle of permissions assigned to an account; `account` is the identity a caller presents. No separate developer/user concept -- what distinguishes work is which door a change goes through: dashboard configuration through the one interface (role-governed), roles and packages as source-only (no role reaches them), a tile's source through the registry.

D3.text: An account lives outside dashboard configuration. Account, then role, then permissions, resolved on every call. Keeps credentials out of dashboard data.

D4.text: Every request resolves to a role at one enforcement point; no caller skips it, including local ones. Rejected: role checks on agent calls only, with human-trusted client endpoints -- that rebuilds the second door D1 removed.

D8.text: A tile carries no placement of its own -- which dashboard, what order, what size all live on the dashboard's reference to it. Makes a tile portable across dashboards, which is what makes more than one dashboard possible later. A tile does carry its own state (D18).

D9.text: A dashboard is an ordered set of tile references. More than one dashboard over one pool of tiles falls out for free, though not built yet.

D11.text: A query names the integration it runs against; the two travel together, no third entity binds them. Two queries against the same integration run separately and hold their own result copies -- nothing is deduplicated or pooled, except the tile mapper each names (D38).

D13.text: Every write is a mutation -- a named change applied against current state, not a snapshot comparison. No revision field, no schema version, no ETag: a queued write that replays late still applies correctly because it describes a change, not a result.

D14.text: Two operations: read a scope, apply mutations atomically. Mutation types are a tagged union, each carrying its required permission category, so enforcement is one lookup and the offline queue is a list of apply payloads. `apply` reports applied or queued, because the interface otherwise promises atomic application online and replay offline while telling a caller neither -- leaving every caller to infer it from its own idea of connectivity. Rejected: a wide RPC surface (`addTile`, `moveTile`, ...) -- each action would need its own route and permission check.

D15.text: Mutations touching integrations require a live connection; every other mutation queues offline and replays on reconnect. The line is security, not structure: an external authorization applied blind against unseen state is the one case where 'apply against whatever you find' is wrong.

D16.text: Integrations and backup targets are one concern. Both are user-authorized connections to an external service, the authorization path is identical, and they differ only in data direction. Split later only if a second concern actually diverges.

D18.text: A tile has state, updated by mutations regardless of what produced them -- no separate entity for what a tile draws from, and no term for one. No tile type, no manual-vs-connected distinction. State is stored already fitting the schema, so rendering is a straight read.

D19.text: No mutation reaches a role -- roles are a source-only change. The `roles` permission category survives read-only in effect; no no-widening guard is needed since nothing can widen a caller's own bundle. Settings doesn't edit roles.

D20.text: Four categories (`data`, `tiles`, `integrations`, `roles`), each holding one ranked level (`noAccess < read < edit < write`, each implying the ones below). No category for appearance, since appearance is served per user from the registry rather than mutated through this interface, which would leave one nothing to gate. The split falls on the mutation, not the category -- `data: edit` alongside `tiles: edit` lets a caller change what a tile shows without adding or deleting tiles. One decision takes the mutation type, the acting account, and the target's owner, and returns allow or deny; ownership is an input to it rather than a second rule beside it, so one lookup genuinely decides.

D21.text: One dashboard ships, with no create/delete mutation. It arrives in the default configuration so 'no dashboard exists' is never a state the UI handles.

D24.text: A dashboard serves its own tiles as a registry, so discovery happens through `shadcn search` / `view` / `add` rather than a bespoke tool an agent must first be taught. Sourced from what `shadcn build` produced, never a directory scan or an index assembled at request time -- a build has temp files and failed candidates that are not real tiles.

D29.text: An integration is shared and defined once; authorization is per-user -- two people on the same service share one integration, not two. Queries are user-specific; results are shared once mapped into tile state. Deliberate privacy posture: authorizing an integration contributes its data to a shared surface, not a private view.

D30.text: When two users' queries write the same tile, the most recent write wins -- no merge, no staleness check, consistent with D13. A known ceiling, not a claim that conflicts don't matter. A refresh runs under the relevant user's credential. A user may only supply queries under their own identity, enforced at the one enforcement point.

D31.text: A query is private to the user who supplied it; only its result is shared (D29). A query reveals more than its result does -- whose calendar, filtered how -- so making results common was deliberate; making search terms common was not. Refresh runs server-side under the owner's credential, so read-visibility doesn't gate whether another user's query runs.

D32.text: A query belongs to its user, never the tile; only the owner reaches it, plus an administrator for deletion.

D35.text: The permission matrix governs shared and server-owned things only. A user's queries, connections, and appearance are allowed to them without reference to a level -- but that comes out of the one decision in D20, which takes the target's owner as an input, rather than from a carve-out sitting beside the matrix. Two default roles ship as ordinary configuration, not fixed names. Roles are edited by editing the file the source imports -- same trust level as editing source. The local machine's own user resolves to full permissions; anyone else starts with none until authenticated. Loopback alone is not proof, since another account on the same host can reach the port.

D38.text: A tile mapper (Fowler's mapper) sets up a correspondence between two schemas without formatting anything; named for what it maps to, since what it maps from is any structured data, not only an API response. A mapper is `"identity"` or a plain function typed against the schema, gated by the same typecheck as a registry item's own source. Rejected: a declarative mapping spec with field renaming, fallback chains, defaults, and array mapping -- its interface was nearly as large as its implementation, and worse, it was a mechanism no model has seen, so every model would learn it from project documentation. That is the divergence D44 exists to remove, and specifying one would contradict the product principle in ARCHITECTURE.md. Mappers live in one shared store referenced by name -- two queries needing the same mapping name the same mapper rather than duplicating it. Adding one is allowed to anyone, since a user who can't write one can't render their own query at all; a referenced mapper has no single owner, so changing or deleting one falls back to the level, and deleting a referenced one always fails instead of cascading.

D40.text: The integration list is project-wide and outlives any one user's connection to it. An entry carries whether it's default, recommended, or dynamic, and its availability. Disconnecting destroys a user's credential immediately; a dynamic entry with zero connections expires after the retention period in project policy. Blocking prevents new connections and refreshes but keeps everything stored, with a notice to affected users. Removing with live dependencies needs an explicit override after a warning -- counts and effects only, never another user's query text, identity, or credential. Expiry runs at startup and on connection change; no background scheduler.

D44.text: Vocabulary conformance is the product, not tidiness. A coined term forces an agent to read project documentation, and reading comprehension is where models diverge most; a shadcn term is already in every model's weights. Three rules follow: this project defines no term shadcn defines, contradicts nothing shadcn documents, and never gives a second name to a meaning shadcn already has. The placed thing is a `tile` rather than a card, because `Card` is a shadcn component and shadcn's own eval prompts use 'cards in a grid' for what this project places. There is no project noun for the reusable half at all -- a registry item's own type names it, and `template` is a CLI flag. Anything the project would have to define to restate a shadcn term is a defect, not a convenience.

D45.text: A tile reference carries `size: sm | md | lg` and nothing else. Rejected: twelve-column integer spans -- expressiveness the common prompts ('make it wider', 'put these side by side', 'full width') never ask for, and every extra option is another axis on which two models disagree. Twelve choices means twelve defensible answers to one instruction. A string enum rather than a number, because that is the form models have most exposure to in this library's context. Maps to real grid spans internally; the agent never sees the integer.

D46.text: A registry item carries its data schema as JSON Schema in `meta`. That pairing is the whole contract an agent writes against, and it is the one thing in this area shadcn has no opinion about -- everything else is already registry vocabulary. The browser converts that schema to a validator at load rather than reading a map compiled in at build time, so a tile added while the app is running renders without a rebuild. Measured at roughly 13 kB gzipped on top of a validator already shipping for other reasons -- smaller than one charting component, and invisible to a model, which writes TSX and a schema and never sees where validation runs. Rejected: a second validator library alongside the existing one; server-only validation, which saves nothing since the existing validator ships regardless. Correctness of the source itself comes from typechecking against real component types, not a hand-maintained prop schema -- and the component's props type is derived from `meta.schema`, so the same typecheck covers the pairing. Typechecking the source alone proved it valid against shadcn's types while proving nothing about the schema it ships with, which let an item pass every gate and still declare data its component never reads.

D48.text: One npm package, no workspaces, one project-root `components.json`. Rejected: shadcn's monorepo layout. Its benefit is the CLI deciding file placement, and that already happens in a single package -- `aliases.ui` and `aliases.components` are separate targets, which is what routes base components one way and blocks the other. A workspace boundary relocates those targets; it does not create the split. What it adds is cost: `@workspace/ui/...` is a far rarer import shape than `@/components/ui/...`, and a path shape models have seen less often is one they reproduce less consistently, which runs against D44. Plus two config files whose `style`, `iconLibrary`, `baseColor`, and aliases must agree, npm workspaces, and Turborepo -- for one consuming app. Revisit if a second app appears. `package.json#imports` is not an alternative to any of this; it is an alias mechanism inside a monorepo, replacing `tsconfig.json` paths and nothing else.

D47.text: Credentials are referenced by name in `${NAME}` form, following shadcn's registry-authentication convention. Resolution takes the name and the acting account together: one dashboard holds many people's credentials for the same integration, and an environment variable has one value per process, so a name alone cannot tell them apart. That makes the seam real rather than hypothetical -- an in-memory adapter for tests, an encrypted source in use. The configuration holds a name, never a secret; the value comes from an encrypted source, and rotation belongs to that source. Rejected: storing sealed material here -- that is what forces a rotation schedule, per-secret key naming to avoid a flag day, and a swappable secret-box seam. Store none of it and none of that is needed. Multi-user follows from the server resolving a presented credential to an identity, which is the documented pattern, and needs no project-specific auth vocabulary.
